analysis.one_liner: Lets states veto endangered species listings and pays landowners when protections lower property values.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2016 with no cosponsors and died in the House Natural Resources Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the Endangered Species Act so that no species could be added to the protected list unless every state it lives in agrees and Congress votes to approve the whole list, and any listing would expire automatically after five years. It would let governors take over protection of species found only within their state — with no court able to review their decisions — and would pay property owners 150 percent of their land's value when a federal action for a protected species cuts its value. It would also stop citizens from petitioning to protect species and from collecting attorney fees when they sue to enforce the law.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and developers of land that might harbor protected species benefit most: the bill gives them a 90-day window after which any proposed land use is deemed legal even if the Interior Department never answers, and it pays them 150 percent of fair market value if a protection decision lowers their property's value. Electric power customers and the federal power administrations gain from itemized billing of species-compliance costs, and states gain control over species found only within their borders.

how_it_helps.text: Any owner or lessee of real property can get a determination on whether a proposed use violates the ESA, and if Interior fails to respond within 90 days the use is deemed legal; a determination is also an affirmative defense to penalties [S2][S3].

If Interior determines a proposed use will violate the ESA, the owner or lessee can seek compensation equal to 150 percent of the property's fair market value when an agency action diminishes that value by 50 percent or more [S3].

Governors of states where a species is found only within that state's borders may take over its regulation with exclusive authority over permits, critical habitat, and recovery plans, and their actions cannot be reviewed by any federal or state court [S2][S3].

The Bonneville, Southeastern, Southwestern, and Western power administrations must tell customers on their monthly bills what share of their costs comes from complying with the ESA, and agencies must disclose their litigation expenditures in a public database [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, taxpayers would pay the 150 percent compensation claims and higher administrative costs, and the public would lose protections for species: listings would need every affected state's consent and a congressional vote, would expire after five years, could no longer be started by citizen petitions, and citizen suits could no longer recover attorney fees. Protected species and the ecosystems that depend on them would bear the cost of weaker, politicized, and time-limited protection.

drawbacks.text: Species listings would require the consent of every governor of every state where the species is present and a joint resolution of Congress before taking effect, and would be removed automatically after five years unless Congress reapproves them [S2][S3].

The bill would eliminate the citizen petition process for adding or removing species and would strike attorney-fee awards in ESA citizen suits, removing two of the main tools citizens have to enforce the law [S2][S3].

State governors' decisions on intrastate species would be exempt from judicial review in any federal or state court, so no one could challenge them, and the bill's own findings frame ESA regulation as a tool that environmentalists use to block projects [S3].

Paying owners 150 percent of fair market value out of federal funds whenever a species-related agency action cuts a property's intended-use value by half or more would create a large, open-ended taxpayer liability [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's cost-disclosure and transparency provisions have some appeal, but its core design dismantles the listing system: a single governor or a stalled Congress could block any listing, protections would lapse every five years, landowners could proceed after an unanswered 90-day notice, and taxpayers would owe 150 percent compensation. Honest supporters would acknowledge that species found in a single reluctant state would effectively lose federal protection entirely.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Blaine Luetkemeyer introduced the bill on May 18, 2016, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day [S1][S5].
No cosponsors ever joined the bill [S4].
The committee took no further action, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Protected species and the existing Endangered Species Act framework were better off because the bill died; no landowner compensation obligations or state veto over listings were created. The status quo, which had drawn no cosponsors to this rewrite, prevailed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Species protections and the existing ESA framework

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and the bill's only recorded support was its single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would give them a deemed-compliance safe harbor after 90 days of federal silence and pay them 150 percent of fair market value when species protections cut a property's value — costs that shift to taxpayers. The gain comes directly at the expense of habitat protection on private land.

The bill would eliminate the citizen petition process, attorney-fee awards in citizen suits, and congressional approval requirements that let litigation drive listings, removing their main enforcement levers.

industries.industry: Electric utilities and federal power administrations
industries.note: The bill would require itemized disclosure of ESA compliance costs on customer bills and in public reports — transparency that mostly serves customers — though it would also exempt intrastate species from those disclosures.
